questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is 5 days post anterior resection. He develops fever 38.7°C, tachycardia, abdominal pain and feculent fluid in his drain.
questions.explanation: Anastomotic leak — classically days 5–7, with pain, fever, tachycardia and feculent drainage. A major cause of post-operative mortality. Management: resuscitate, antibiotics, CT with contrast, then radiological drainage or return to theatre depending on stability. The post-op fever timeline (the 'five Ws') places respiratory causes days 1–2, UTI 3–5, DVT 4–6, wound 5–7.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has a tibial fracture. Six hours later he has severe pain worsened by passive toe extension, and a tense swollen calf. Distal pulses are palpable.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure — palpable pulses exclude compartment syndrome
Elevate the limb and reassess in 4 hours
questions.explanation: Acute compartment syndrome — pain out of proportion, worse on passive stretch, tense compartment. Pulses are usually present, because compartment pressure exceeds venous but not arterial pressure; pulselessness is a very late sign and waiting for it costs the limb. Treatment is urgent fasciotomy. Elevation above heart level reduces perfusion and is avoided.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has vomiting and drowsiness. Glucose 24, pH 7.12, bicarbonate 9, ketones 5.4. Potassium is 3.1.
options: IV fluids and potassium replacement before starting insulin
questions.explanation: The potassium is low. Insulin drives K⁺ intracellularly and will precipitate dangerous, potentially fatal hypokalaemia. Give fluids and replace potassium first — insulin is typically withheld until K⁺ ≥3.5, or run alongside replacement. Bicarbonate is not routine in DKA even with marked acidosis; it worsens paradoxical CNS acidosis.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with painless obstructive jaundice, weight loss, and a palpable non-tender gallbladder.
questions.lead: What does the palpable gallbladder suggest?
options: Gallstone disease — the commonest cause of jaundice
questions.explanation: Courvoisier's law: a palpable, non-tender gallbladder with jaundice is unlikely to be due to stones — chronic stone disease produces a fibrotic, non-distensible gallbladder. Painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss points to malignancy of the pancreatic head (or distal biliary tree). Cholecystitis and cholangitis are painful and febrile.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with COPD has a routine ABG: pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 58mmHg, HCO₃ 32, PaO₂ 62mmHg on room air.
options: Acute respiratory acidosis requiring urgent NIV
questions.explanation: pH is near-normal despite a markedly raised CO₂, with a correspondingly raised bicarbonate — that is chronic respiratory acidosis with renal metabolic compensation. Renal compensation takes days, so its presence tells you this is chronic. An acute rise in CO₂ would give a low pH with a normal bicarbonate. Target SpO₂ 88–92% in this patient.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman on long-term prednisolone for rheumatoid arthritis is admitted for emergency laparotomy.
questions.lead: What additional perioperative management is required?
options: No change — continue her usual oral dose
Stop steroids to reduce infection risk
questions.explanation: Long-term exogenous steroid suppresses the HPA axis, so she cannot mount the cortisol surge that major surgery demands — without stress-dose cover she risks adrenal crisis intraoperatively. Stopping steroids abruptly is the opposite of what is required. This is the surgical face of secondary adrenal insufficiency.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation presents with painless bright red PV bleeding of about 250mL. The uterus is soft and non-tender; CTG is normal.
questions.explanation: Painless bleeding with a soft non-tender uterus suggests placenta praevia. A digital vaginal examination can disrupt a low-lying placenta and cause catastrophic haemorrhage — it is avoided in any antepartum haemorrhage until praevia is excluded by ultrasound. Speculum examination is acceptable. Contrast with abruption: painful bleeding, tender woody uterus, loss often concealed.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has an incidental 3cm left adrenal mass on CT performed for trauma. He is normotensive and asymptomatic.
questions.lead: What is the essential first step?
options: Biochemical evaluation for hormone excess, including exclusion of phaeochromocytoma
questions.explanation: Every adrenal incidentaloma needs functional assessment — overnight dexamethasone suppression, aldosterone/renin ratio if hypertensive or hypokalaemic, and plasma metanephrines — plus assessment of malignant risk by size and imaging characteristics. Biopsy is contraindicated before excluding phaeochromocytoma, since it can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. Surgery follows the results, not the other way round.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman on warfarin falls and hits her head. She is alert, GCS 15, with no focal deficit. INR is 2.8.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate management?
options: CT head, and observe even if the initial scan is normal
Reverse warfarin immediately regardless of imaging
questions.explanation: Anticoagulation is an independent indication for CT head after any head injury, even with GCS 15 and no deficit — and a period of observation is warranted even with a normal initial scan, because delayed intracranial haemorrhage is well described in anticoagulated patients. Reversal is only indicated if bleeding is demonstrated; reversing prophylactically exposes her to thrombotic risk.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis has ascites. Diagnostic paracentesis shows an ascitic neutrophil count of 340 cells/mm³.
questions.lead: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
options: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis — IV antibiotics and albumin
questions.explanation: An ascitic neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ diagnoses spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, regardless of culture result. Treat with IV antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporin) plus IV albumin, which reduces hepatorenal syndrome and mortality. Secondary bacterial peritonitis (from a perforated viscus) is suggested by polymicrobial culture, very high protein, and multiple organisms — that one needs surgery.
